0.title: Dead to Sin, Alive to God
0.overview:
Every honest Christian knows the struggle. We love Christ and want to please him, and yet we keep falling into the same sins: a sharp tongue, a lustful look, a jealous thought, a habit we have confessed a hundred times. Some Christians despair, wondering whether they are really saved. Others give up the fight and make peace with their sin. Neither is the Bible's way.

Scripture is realistic. It never pretends that Christians are sinless in this life. If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us (1 John 1:8). But it is also hopeful. Sin no longer rules the believer. The Spirit lives in us. Christ has broken sin's power, and he will one day remove its presence. In between, there is a real fight, and it is a fight we are equipped to win.

This study is not a list of techniques. The battle against sin is won by grace, through union with Christ, by the power of the Spirit, using the means God has given. But it is a battle, and it requires effort, honesty, wisdom and the help of other believers.

Six units: (1) Why Christians Still Sin; (2) Dead to Sin, Alive to God; (3) How Temptation Works; (4) Putting Sin to Death; (5) Fighting Together; (6) When You Fall. The study belongs with the Holiness of God and Forgiveness & Reconciliation studies.

1.title: Why Christians Still Sin
1.overview:
When we become Christians, we are forgiven, justified and adopted. We are given new hearts and the Holy Spirit. So why do we still sin?

Sin remains, though it no longer reigns. At conversion, sin's dominion is broken. For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace (Rom 6:14). But sin's presence remains. Paul calls it the flesh: the old sinful nature that still clings to us and fights against the Spirit. For the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh, for these are opposed to each other (Gal 5:17). Every believer has a civil war inside.

The struggle is a sign of life. Paul describes this inner conflict with painful honesty: For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate (Rom 7:15). Before conversion, most people do not struggle much with sin; they simply follow their desires. The fact that you hate your sin and fight it is evidence that the Spirit is at work in you. Dead people do not struggle.

Sin is deceitful. Sin never presents itself honestly. It promises pleasure, freedom or relief, and hides its cost. It makes excuses: "Just this once." "No one will know." "You deserve it." "It's not that bad." Hebrews warns against being hardened by the deceitfulness of sin (Heb 3:13). Part of fighting sin is learning to see through its lies.

We live in a fallen world. Sin is not only within us. We face a world system that celebrates what God forbids, and a real enemy, the devil, who tempts and accuses (1 Pet 5:8). The flesh, the world and the devil work together.

The fight will last until glory. No Christian reaches sinless perfection in this life. But the fight is not hopeless. Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! (Rom 7:25). Sanctification is real and progressive. The Christian who has walked with God for forty years should be more like Christ than when he began, though he will feel his sin more keenly than ever.
1.theology:
Romans 7: the views. Some read Romans 7:14-25 as Paul describing his life before conversion, or a person under conviction trying to keep the law in his own strength. Others read it as the normal experience of a mature believer who delights in God's law but still finds sin at work in him.

The verdict: Paul is describing his life as a believer. He uses the present tense throughout. He says I delight in the law of God, in my inner being (Rom 7:22), which no unregenerate person does (Rom 8:7). And the passage ends not in despair but in thanksgiving to God through Christ. Romans 7 is not a picture of defeat, but of the honest struggle of every believer, which Romans 8 then answers with the power of the Spirit.

New people with old habits: Believers have a new heart, but the old nature has not been removed. We are new people with old habits. Sanctification is the process of becoming in practice what we already are in Christ.
1.examples:
Then: David was a man after God's own heart, who wrote psalms of deep devotion. Yet he committed adultery with Bathsheba and arranged her husband's murder (2 Sam 11). His fall is a warning that no believer is beyond the reach of temptation.

Now: A young Christian is shocked to find that after his conversion he still struggles with anger. He wonders if his faith was real. An older believer tells him, "The fact that you are troubled by it is a good sign. Before, you would not have cared." He begins to fight his anger with hope instead of despair.

A simple test: Do you hate your sin, or only its consequences? Hatred of sin itself is a mark of the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate. Now if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law, that it is good. So now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me. For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out. For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing. Now if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me. So I find it to be a law that when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand. For I delight in the law of God, in my inner being, but I see in my members another law waging war against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin that dwells in my members. Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's honesty is startling. The great apostle admits that he does what he hates and fails to do what he wants. He traces this to sin that dwells within me. Yet he also says he delights in God's law. His cry, Wretched man that I am!, is the cry of every believer who feels the pull of sin. And the answer comes at once: deliverance through Jesus Christ our Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. For the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh, for these are opposed to each other, to keep you from doing the things you want to do. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul describes two opposing forces within the believer: the flesh and the Spirit. They are at war. But he does not leave it as a stalemate. Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. The flesh is still present, but it need not win.

verseByVerse.quote: If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. If we say we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: John rules out two errors. Some claim to have no sin; they deceive themselves. Others claim never to have sinned; they make God a liar. The honest Christian admits his sin and confesses it, and finds God faithful and just to forgive. Pretending to be sinless is far more dangerous than admitting we are not.

verseByVerse.quote: Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil, unbelieving heart, leading you to fall away from the living God. But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called "today," that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The writer warns against an unbelieving heart that turns away from God. How does this happen? Through being hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. Sin deceives gradually, and the heart hardens slowly. The remedy is daily mutual encouragement. We need others to help us see through sin's lies.

1.reflection:
What is the difference between sin remaining and sin reigning in a believer?

Read Romans 7:14-25. Where do you recognise your own experience?

What lies does sin most often tell you?

How does the struggle against sin show that the Spirit is at work in you?

2.title: Dead to Sin, Alive to God
2.overview:
The fight against sin begins not with what we do but with who we are in Christ. Paul's great chapter on holiness, Romans 6, does not start with commands. It starts with facts.

We died with Christ. We know that our old self was crucified with him in order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin (Rom 6:6). When Christ died, believers died with him. The old self, the person we were in Adam, enslaved to sin, has been put to death. Sin's claim on us has been cancelled.

We were raised with Christ. We too might walk in newness of life (Rom 6:4). We share Christ's resurrection life now. We are new creations (2 Cor 5:17). The Spirit who raised Jesus lives in us.

So consider yourselves dead to sin. Only after stating these facts does Paul give the first command: So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus (Rom 6:11). This is not pretending. It is believing what is true. Many Christians fight sin as if they were still its slaves. Paul says: you are free. Live like it.

So do not let sin reign. Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions (Rom 6:12). Sin is a deposed tyrant still trying to give orders. Believers do not have to obey. We are to present our bodies to God as instruments for righteousness.

Set your minds on things above. Colossians follows the same pattern. If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is (Col 3:1). Our life is hidden with Christ in God. The way to fight earthly desires is to fill our minds with heavenly realities: Christ's love, his glory, his return and our future with him.

This is the foundation. Holiness is not trying to become someone we are not. It is becoming in practice who we already are in Christ.
2.theology:
Indicative before imperative: Throughout the New Testament, commands (imperatives) rest on facts (indicatives): now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light (Eph 5:8). Because you have been raised with Christ, seek the things above (Col 3:1). The order matters. Commands without the gospel crush us. The gospel without commands leaves us passive. Together they transform.

Definitive and progressive sanctification: Sanctification has two aspects. Definitively, believers have been set apart once for all as God's holy people, and sin's dominion has been broken. Progressively, believers are being made holy day by day. The first guarantees the second.

Union with Christ: Everything in this unit flows from union with Christ. We died with him, were raised with him, are hidden in him and will appear with him. Sanctification is not a self-help project but the life of Christ in us.
2.examples:
Then: The Israelites, freed from slavery in Egypt, kept wanting to go back. They even said, Let us choose a leader and go back to Egypt (Num 14:4). Freedom takes time to sink in. Believers too must learn to live as the free people they are.

Now: A woman who struggles with gossip has always fought it by trying harder not to talk. Studying Romans 6, she begins each morning by reminding herself: "I died with Christ. I am alive to God. My tongue belongs to him." She still fails at times. But her fight now starts from freedom, not from fear.

A simple test: When you fight sin, do you begin with "I must try harder" or with "In Christ I am free"?

verseByVerse.quote: What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in it? Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul anticipates an objection: if grace abounds where sin increases, should we keep sinning? His answer is horror: By no means! We died to sin. Baptism signifies our union with Christ in death and resurrection. Continuing in sin is not only wrong; it is a contradiction of who we are.

verseByVerse.quote: So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus. Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions. Do not present your members to sin as instruments for unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life, and your members to God as instruments for righteousness. For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The first command in Romans 6 is to think rightly: consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God. Then come the practical commands: do not let sin reign; do not present your members to sin; present yourselves to God. The promise underpins it all: sin will not be your master, because you are under grace.

verseByVerse.quote: If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul points believers upward. Christ is seated at God's right hand, and our life is hidden with him. One day he will appear, and we will appear with him in glory. Setting our minds on these things is not escapism. It is the power for holiness, because what we love most shapes how we live.

verseByVerse.quote: For the love of Christ controls us, because we have concluded this: that one has died for all, therefore all have died; and he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised. From now on, therefore, we regard no one according to the flesh. Even though we once regarded Christ according to the flesh, we regard him thus no longer. Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Christ's love controls us. He died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him. Believers are a new creation: the old has passed away, the new has come. The motive for holiness is not fear but gratitude to the One who died and was raised for us.

2.reflection:
What does it mean that your "old self was crucified" with Christ?

Why does Paul state facts before he gives commands in Romans 6?

How could you "set your mind on things above" in a moment of temptation?

Write down one sin you struggle with. How does Romans 6:11 speak to it?

3.title: How Temptation Works
3.overview:
Understanding how temptation works helps us resist it. Scripture gives a clear picture.

Temptation begins within. But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death (Jas 1:14-15). James describes a process: desire, enticement, conception, birth, growth, death. The fruit of sin is death. And the root is our own desire. We cannot blame God: God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one (Jas 1:13). Nor can we blame circumstances or others entirely.

The first temptation. In Eden, the serpent began by questioning God's word: Did God actually say...? (Gen 3:1). Then he denied God's warning and slandered God's character, suggesting God was holding back something good (Gen 3:4-5). Then the woman saw that the fruit was good for food, a delight to the eyes and desirable to make one wise (Gen 3:6). Temptation still works this way. It doubts God's word, distrusts God's goodness and makes sin look attractive.

How Jesus resisted. In the wilderness, Jesus faced temptation after forty days of fasting. Each time he answered from Scripture: It is written (Matt 4:4, 7, 10). He did not argue with the devil or rely on his feelings. He held to God's word. Where Adam fell in a garden with every provision, Jesus stood in a wilderness with none.

Temptation is not sin. Jesus was tempted in every respect... as we are, yet without sin (Heb 4:15). Feeling the pull of temptation is not the same as sinning. The sin comes when we entertain, welcome and act on the desire. This is a great comfort to sensitive consciences.

God provides a way out. No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it (1 Cor 10:13). No temptation is unique to you. None is irresistible. And God always provides a way of escape. Often the way out is simple: leave the room, close the app, call a friend, pray.
3.theology:
Know your weak points: Temptation often comes when we are hungry, angry, lonely or tired. Jesus was tempted when he was hungry. David fell when he was idle at home while his army was at war (2 Sam 11:1). Knowing our vulnerable moments helps us prepare.

The devil's role: Satan is real and active, but he is not all-powerful. He cannot force a believer to sin. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you (Jas 4:7). He is a defeated enemy (Col 2:15).

Pray against temptation: Jesus taught us to pray, lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil (Matt 6:13). Prayer is not a last resort; it is a first line of defence. In Gethsemane he told his disciples, Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation (Matt 26:41). They slept, and fell.
3.examples:
Then: Joseph was tempted day after day by Potiphar's wife. He refused, saying, How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God? (Gen 39:9). When she grabbed him, he ran, leaving his cloak behind. He saw sin as an offence against God, and he did not linger.

Now: A man notices that he is most tempted to look at pornography late at night when he is tired and alone with his phone. He decides to charge his phone outside the bedroom and to go to bed at a set time. He also tells a trusted friend. The temptation does not disappear, but the moments of greatest weakness are guarded.

A simple test: When are you most vulnerable to temptation? What is one practical step to guard that moment?

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one say when he is tempted, "I am being tempted by God," for God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one. But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: James refuses to let us blame God for temptation. God is not tempted by evil and does not tempt anyone. Temptation arises from our own desires, which lure us like bait. Sin grows step by step, and its end is death. The best time to resist is at the beginning, before desire conceives.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the serpent was more crafty than any other beast of the field that the LORD God had made. He said to the woman, "Did God actually say, 'You shall not eat of any tree in the garden'?" And the woman said to the serpent, "We may eat of the fruit of the trees in the garden, but God said, 'You shall not eat of the fruit of the tree that is in the midst of the garden, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.'" But the serpent said to the woman, "You will not surely die. For God knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil." So when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The serpent's strategy is subtle. He questions God's word, contradicts God's warning, and suggests that God is keeping something good from them. Then the fruit looks good, pleasant and desirable. The woman eats and gives some to her husband, who is with her. Every temptation since has followed a similar pattern.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. And after fasting forty days and forty nights, he was hungry. And the tempter came and said to him, "If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread." But he answered, "It is written, "'Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.'" Then the devil took him to the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple and said to him, "If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, for it is written, "'He will command his angels concerning you,' and "'On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.'" Jesus said to him, "Again it is written, 'You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.'" Again, the devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. And he said to him, "All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me." Then Jesus said to him, "Be gone, Satan! For it is written, "'You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve.'" Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and were ministering to him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted. The devil tempted him to satisfy hunger, to test God and to gain the world by worshipping Satan. Each time Jesus answered with Scripture from Deuteronomy. He succeeded where Israel failed in the wilderness, and where Adam failed in the garden. His victory is ours by faith, and his method is our model.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall. No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul warns the overconfident: let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall. Then he comforts the fearful: no temptation is unique, God is faithful, and he always provides a way of escape. Pride is dangerous; despair is unnecessary. God's faithfulness is the guarantee.

3.reflection:
Trace the steps of temptation in James 1:14-15. Where in the process is it easiest to resist?

How does the serpent's strategy in Genesis 3 still work today?

Which Bible verses could you memorise to answer your most common temptations, as Jesus did?

What is the "way of escape" God most often provides for you?

4.title: Putting Sin to Death
4.overview:
The Bible's language for fighting sin is violent. Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry (Col 3:5). If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away (Matt 5:29). This is not a call to self-harm, but to radical seriousness. Sin is not a pet to be managed but an enemy to be killed.

By the Spirit. For if you live according to the flesh you will die, but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live (Rom 8:13). We do the putting to death, but we do it by the Spirit. We cannot do it in our own strength. But the Spirit does not do it without us. Grace does not make us passive; it makes us active.

Put off and put on. Paul's method is not just removal but replacement. Believers are taught to put off your old self and to put on the new self (Eph 4:22, 24). The thief should not merely stop stealing but work and give (Eph 4:28). The liar should not merely stop lying but speak truth (Eph 4:25). An empty heart will soon be filled again with sin. A heart filled with love for Christ crowds sin out.

Flee. Some sins should not be fought but fled. So flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace (2 Tim 2:22). Flee from sexual immorality (1 Cor 6:18). Wisdom does not stand near the edge of a cliff to prove it will not fall.

Use the means of grace. God has given ordinary means to strengthen believers: his word (I have stored up your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you, Ps 119:11), prayer, the Lord's Supper, fellowship and worship. These are not magic, but they are how the Spirit normally works. A Christian who neglects them is fighting with no weapons.

Make no provision. But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires (Rom 13:14). Do not plan for sin. Remove what feeds it: the websites, the company, the habits, the hidden stash.
4.theology:
How are we sanctified? The views. Some teach that believers can reach a state of sinless perfection in this life. Others teach a "higher life" approach: stop striving and simply surrender, "let go and let God," and Christ will live the victorious life through you. Others stress human effort and discipline, sometimes with little reference to grace.

The verdict: Sanctification is God's work in which we actively cooperate. Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Phil 2:12-13). We work because God works. Perfection is never reached in this life (1 John 1:8), and passivity is never commanded. The New Testament is full of commands to put off, put to death, flee, strive and pursue.

Heart and habits: Fighting sin requires changing both our desires and our habits. Behaviour change without heart change produces Pharisees. Heart change without new habits produces frustration. The Spirit works on both.
4.examples:
Then: When the Ephesian believers turned to Christ, many who had practised magic brought their books and burned them publicly, books worth fifty thousand pieces of silver (Acts 19:19). They did not keep them in a drawer just in case. Repentance was decisive and costly.

Now: A woman struggles with envy whenever she looks at friends' lives on social media. She deletes the apps from her phone for a season. In their place, she starts a habit of writing down three things she is thankful for each evening. Over months, envy weakens and gratitude grows. She has put off and put on.

A simple test: Is there anything in your life that feeds a sin you are fighting? What would it mean to make no provision for it?

verseByVerse.quote: So then, brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh you will die, but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live. For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Believers owe nothing to the flesh. Living by it leads to death. But putting to death the deeds of the body by the Spirit leads to life. And those who are led by the Spirit in this way are sons of God. The fight against sin is itself evidence of adoption.

verseByVerse.quote: Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry. On account of these the wrath of God is coming. In these you too once walked, when you were living in them. But now you must put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth. Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old self with its practices and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul lists sins to put to death, beginning with sexual sins and ending with covetousness, which he calls idolatry. Then he lists sins of speech to put away. The reason: believers have put off the old self and put on the new, which is being renewed in the image of its Creator. Holiness is the restoration of God's image in us.

verseByVerse.quote: "You have heard that it was said, 'You shall not commit adultery.' But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart. If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body be thrown into hell. And if your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body go into hell. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus takes the seventh commandment to the heart: lustful looking is adultery of the heart. Then he gives a vivid command: cut off what causes you to sin. This is hyperbole, but its point is deadly serious. Better to lose something precious than to lose your soul. Radical sin requires radical measures.

verseByVerse.quote: How can a young man keep his way pure? By guarding it according to your word. With my whole heart I seek you; let me not wander from your commandments! I have stored up your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The psalmist asks how a young man can keep his way pure. The answer is guarding it according to God's word. He seeks God with his whole heart and stores God's word in his heart so that he will not sin. Memorising and meditating on Scripture is one of the strongest weapons against temptation.

4.reflection:
Why does the Bible use such violent language about sin?

What does it mean to put sin to death "by the Spirit" (Rom 8:13)?

Choose a sin you are fighting. What should you "put off" and what should you "put on"?

Which means of grace do you most neglect? How could you begin using it again?

5.title: Fighting Together
5.overview:
Many Christians fight sin alone, in secret. They are ashamed to tell anyone, so they confess privately to God, make private resolutions and fail privately again. Scripture calls us to a different path. The fight against sin is meant to be fought together.

Confess to one another. Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed (Jas 5:16). Confession to God brings forgiveness. Confession to a trusted believer brings healing, accountability and prayer. Sin thrives in darkness. When it is brought into the light, it loses much of its power.

Exhort one another daily. But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called "today," that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin (Heb 3:13). We need people who will ask us hard questions and speak truth to us. Sin is deceptive, and we are often the last to see our own.

Restore one another gently. Brothers, if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted (Gal 6:1). When others confess to us, we must respond not with shock or gossip, but with gentleness, prayer and practical help, remembering our own weakness.

Choose your company wisely. Do not be deceived: "Bad company ruins good morals" (1 Cor 15:33). Friends shape us. Those who want to grow in holiness should spend time with others who want the same.

The local church. God has placed believers in churches partly for this purpose. Elders watch over souls. Members encourage and warn one another. In serious cases, church discipline is a last resort to call a believer back from persistent sin. A Christian who is isolated from the church is far more vulnerable.

Accountability that works. Effective accountability is honest, regular and grace-filled. It asks specific questions, prays together, celebrates progress and responds to failure with the gospel rather than condemnation. It is not policing, but brotherly love.
5.theology:
Confession to a priest? James 5:16 says to confess to one another, not to a priest who absolves sins. Every believer has direct access to God through Christ. Confession to fellow believers is for mutual help and prayer, not for obtaining forgiveness, which comes from God alone.

Wisdom in confession: Not every sin needs to be confessed to everyone. Sins against a particular person should be confessed to that person. Public sins may need public acknowledgment. Private struggles are best shared with a mature, trusted believer of the same sex.

Grace in community: A church where everyone pretends to be fine will never become a place of healing. Leaders should model honesty about their own struggles, appropriately, so that others feel free to seek help.
5.examples:
Then: When David sinned, God sent Nathan the prophet, who told him a story and then said, You are the man! (2 Sam 12:7). David had hidden his sin for months. One faithful friend with a hard word brought him to repentance.

Now: Three men in a church meet every other week for breakfast. They read Scripture, ask each other honest questions about their marriages, work and private lives, and pray. Over the years, each has confessed sins he had never told anyone. Each has found help and prayer. None has been shamed.

A simple test: Is there one person who knows your real struggles and regularly asks how you are doing?

verseByVerse.quote: Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing praise. Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. And if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven. Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: James pictures a praying community. The suffering pray, the cheerful sing, the sick call the elders. Then he widens it: confess your sins to one another and pray for one another. The prayer of a righteous person is powerful. Healing, in body and soul, often comes through the honest prayers of fellow believers.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted. Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ. For if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself. But let each one test his own work, and then his reason to boast will be in himself alone and not in his neighbor. For each will have to bear his own load. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul gives instructions for restoring a believer caught in sin. Gentleness is required, and self-watchfulness. Bearing one another's burdens fulfils the law of Christ. Yet each must also carry his own load. Mutual help does not remove personal responsibility.

verseByVerse.quote: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil. For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up! Again, if two lie together, they keep warm, but how can one keep warm alone? And though a man might prevail against one who is alone, two will withstand him—a threefold cord is not quickly broken. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Preacher observes that two are better than one. If one falls, the other can lift him up. Woe to the one who falls alone. A threefold cord is not quickly broken. The principle applies to the fight against sin: alone we are vulnerable; together we are strong.

verseByVerse.quote: Better is open rebuke than hidden love. Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Faithful are the wounds of a friend. A true friend will tell us hard truths, even when it hurts. Flattery is easy and pleasant, but it leaves us in our sin. Open rebuke from someone who loves us is better than hidden love that says nothing.

5.reflection:
Why do Christians often fight sin alone? What are the dangers of this?

Who could you ask to be an accountability partner? What questions would you want them to ask?

How should you respond when someone confesses a sin to you?

Read Proverbs 27:5-6. When has a friend's hard word helped you?

6.title: When You Fall
6.overview:
Every believer will fall. The question is what we do next. Two responses are deadly: hiding the sin and despairing of grace. Scripture shows a better way.

Come back quickly. My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1 John 2:1). John does not say "if anyone sins, he is lost." He says we have an advocate. Jesus stands before the Father on our behalf, and his sacrifice is the propitiation for our sins. The way back is always open.

Confess honestly. Psalm 51, David's prayer after his sin with Bathsheba, is a model of repentance. He does not excuse or blame: For I know my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me. Against you, you only, have I sinned (Ps 51:3-4). He appeals to God's mercy, not his own record: Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love (Ps 51:1). He asks for cleansing and a new heart.

Believe the forgiveness. After confession comes the harder part for many: believing that God has forgiven. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9). God does not forgive grudgingly or partially. Do not keep punishing yourself for what Christ has paid for.

Get up again. For the righteous falls seven times and rises again (Prov 24:16). The difference between the righteous and the wicked is not that the righteous never fall, but that they get back up. Rejoice not over me, O my enemy; when I fall, I shall rise (Mic 7:8).

Make amends. Where our sin has harmed others, repentance includes confession to them and, where possible, restitution.

Learn and guard. After a fall, ask what led to it. What were the conditions? What lies did I believe? What practical steps can guard me next time? Repentance is not only sorrow for the past but a change of direction for the future.
6.theology:
Godly grief and worldly grief: For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death (2 Cor 7:10). Worldly grief is sorry about the consequences, the embarrassment or the damage to our image. Godly grief is sorry about offending God, and it turns to him.

Assurance after a fall: A true believer can fall seriously, as David and Peter did, and still be restored. But persistent, unrepentant sin is a warning sign. The response to a fall is not to question every past experience, but to repent and return. The Assurance of Salvation study explores this further.

Discipline from a Father: God sometimes disciplines his children after a fall, through consequences or hardship. This is not punishment but training, a sign of his love (Heb 12:5-11).
6.examples:
Then: Peter denied Jesus three times on the night of his arrest. Jesus had prayed for him: I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers (Luke 22:32). After the resurrection, Jesus restored him publicly. Peter's fall became part of his ministry to others.

Now: A Christian who had been free from drinking for two years relapses after a bad week. His first instinct is to hide it and wallow in shame. Instead, he calls his accountability partner that night, confesses, and they pray together. The next day he tells his wife. He reads Psalm 51 and 1 John 2:1-2. He is not proud of the fall, but he is not crushed by it. He gets up again.

A simple test: When you sin, how long does it usually take before you confess it to God? What would help you come back more quickly?

verseByVerse.quote: Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love; according to your abundant mercy blot out my transgressions. Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin! For I know my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me. Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight, so that you may be justified in your words and blameless in your judgment. Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me. Behold, you delight in truth in the inward being, and you teach me wisdom in the secret heart. Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow. Let me hear joy and gladness; let the bones that you have broken rejoice. Hide your face from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities. Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Cast me not away from your presence, and take not your Holy Spirit from me. Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and uphold me with a willing spirit. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: David's prayer is the great model of repentance. He appeals to God's steadfast love and abundant mercy. He takes full responsibility for his sin. He asks for cleansing, a clean heart and a right spirit. And he longs to have the joy of salvation restored. Repentance does not end in shame but in renewed joy.

verseByVerse.quote: My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: John's goal is that his readers not sin. But he knows they will, so he gives them the gospel. They have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, whose sacrifice turns away God's wrath. The believer who falls is not abandoned. He has the best possible defender.

verseByVerse.quote: "Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers." Peter said to him, "Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death." Jesus said, "I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow this day, until you deny three times that you know me." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus knew Peter would deny him. He warned him and prayed for him. Notice what he prayed: not that Peter would not fall, but that his faith would not fail. And Jesus spoke of his restoration before the fall even happened: when you have turned again. Christ's prayers keep his people through their failures.

verseByVerse.quote: for the righteous falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked stumble in times of calamity. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The righteous person is not one who never falls, but one who keeps rising. Seven times suggests many falls. The wicked stumble into calamity and stay down. The righteous get up, by God's grace, and keep going. Perseverance, not perfection, is the mark of the godly.

6.reflection:
Read Psalm 51. Which phrases could you pray after your own failures?

What is the difference between godly grief and worldly grief?

How does 1 John 2:1-2 give you hope when you sin?

After a fall, what practical steps help you get up and guard against the next one?
